turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doc, I just... I had to come in because I can't take it anymore. It's like I've got this, this actual motor running inside me, right? Just humming and vibrating all day long, from the second I wake up. It never shuts off. It's just go, go, go. 

And the worst part, the absolute worst part, is if I have to sit still anywhere. Like, take church for example. I try to go, I really do, but sitting in those pews... man, it's torture. I feel like the walls are closing in. Or even just sitting in the waiting room out there at the clinic before they called me back to see you! I was pacing, I had to go get a drink of water, I flipped through a magazine but I wasn't even looking at the pages. I just felt completely trapped in that little chair. 

Same thing at home, too. I'll sit on the couch to watch TV, and five minutes later I'm up. I just have to get up or do something, anything, really. If I try to force myself to stay put, it's like I'm gonna explode out of my own skin. I just can't do it, I feel totally boxed in everywhere I go if I have to just sit there...

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently leaving their seat when expected to sit, such as getting up after five minutes of watching TV or pacing in the waiting room.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes intense feelings of restlessness, stating they feel trapped and like they will 'explode out of my own skin' if forced to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient uses the exact phrase of having an 'actual motor running inside me' and being 'go, go, go' all day long.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start feeling like you had this motor running inside you?
turns.patient_response:
Man, I know exactly when it got this bad. Like, maybe I was always a little restless growing up, I don't know, sitting in a classroom wasn't really my thing so I left school pretty early, but this specific feeling? This actual motor just running and running where it's this hard to manage? That started about two years and two months ago. 

I remember the exact timing 'cause it was right around the time my older relative—my granddad—when his health just totally went downhill. He was doing okay on his own, and then he just wasn't. And since I wasn't working a regular job, you know, the family decided it fell on me to go over there and help out. Suddenly I got all these responsibilities dumped on my shoulders. I'm having to fetch his meals, help him up out of his chair, keep the house running, figure out what he needs before he even asks for it... it was just so much all at once. 

And ever since I had to take on all that extra stuff for him, it's like my body just went into overdrive and got stuck there. Two years and two months of just zooming around his house, pacing the floorboards, feeling like if I stop moving everything's gonna fall apart. I try to tell my family about it, you know, I tell them how I feel like I'm vibrating out of my shoes all day, but they just say I'm doing a good job and to keep at it. But they don't get it, doc, it's this engine inside me that fired up the second his health changed and I had to be the one taking care of things, and it just hasn't run out of gas since.

symptom_reasoning.S058: The patient expresses severe physical tension and restlessness, stating they feel like they are 'vibrating out of my shoes all day' and that everything will fall apart if they stop moving.

turns.doctor_question: Were you taking or started on any new medications around the time this restless feeling started?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I wasn't taking anything new. I mean, I don't really take much of anything, to be honest with you. Never have been big on pills or going to the doctor unless something's falling off, you know? And even with granddad getting sick, I was the one giving him his meds—sorting out his pillbox, making sure he took the blue one in the morning and the little white ones at night—but me? No, I wasn't taking a single thing. 

I know some people think maybe it's too much coffee or energy drinks or something, but it's not that either. I might have a cup in the morning, but that's it. It wasn't some new pill or vitamin or whatever that did this to me. It really was just the stress of it all, I swear. Just that sudden switch from kind of doing my own thing, bouncing around a bit, to suddenly being the main guy responsible for another human being's life. That's when the motor kicked on. But meds? Nah, doc, definitely no new meds for me. I've been running on my own fumes this whole time, and let me tell you, it's exhausting, but the engine just won't quit.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes their restless state by stating 'the motor kicked on' and 'the engine just won't quit', which directly matches the symptom of acting as if driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient explicitly attributes the onset of their symptoms to an identifiable stressor, specifically the sudden responsibility of becoming the primary caregiver for their sick grandfather.

turns.doctor_question: Along with this feeling of having a motor running, do you find yourself constantly worrying about various everyday things and having trouble controlling those worries?
turns.patient_response:
Worrying? No, man, it's not really like that. I mean, I know what you mean, like people who sit around chewing their fingernails over the electric bill or fretting about what's gonna happen next week... but that's not me at all. Honestly, to worry about things, you gotta be able to sit still and actually dwell on them, right? And I just don't do that. It's not my brain spinning with all these "what ifs" about granddad or the house or whatever everyday stuff. 

It's more... it's just physical, you know? Like, I'll be up fixing a leaky pipe under the sink, and I'm not doing it because I'm worried the sink is gonna flood the whole kitchen and ruin the floors, I'm just doing it because I walked past the kitchen and I can't just go sit back down on the couch. And then five minutes later I'm out sweeping the porch. I'm not worried the porch is dirty or what the neighbors think, I just gotta be sweeping it. 

So no, I wouldn't say I'm constantly worrying or anything like that. It's not fear or, like, anxious thoughts in my head. My family, they'll see me pacing and they always ask, "Are you stressed about something? What's on your mind?" and I'm always telling them, "Nothing! I just need to go mow the lawn right now this exact second!" I don't lay in bed at night fretting about tomorrow's chores, I just lay there wanting to get up and do the chores right then and there because my legs want to move. So yeah, the worry thing... nah, that's definitely not me. Never really has been. I just do things, I don't sit around and fret about them.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes a constant need to be active and doing things, like fixing pipes or mowing the lawn, and an inability to just sit down.

turns.patient_response:
Unusually what? Like, super happy? On top of the world kind of thing? No, man, definitely not. I mean, I'm not a miserable guy or anything, but I don't get those crazy highs where I think I'm Superman or whatever. 

I know some folks get like that, you know? Like my buddy from back in the day, he'd get these weeks where he was just floating, buying rounds for the whole bar, talking a million miles a minute about how he was gonna start a business selling, I don't even know, custom hubcaps or something. He'd be so pumped up he wouldn't sleep, just totally riding this massive wave of feeling invincible. 

But me? Nah. The motor I got running in me, it's not like that at all. It's not a happy motor, it's just a... well, it's just a motor. It's just physical energy that I gotta burn off. I don't feel unusually great or euphoric or any of that. If anything, it's just annoying. Like, I'm just trying to watch a baseball game on the TV with granddad, and I can't even make it through an inning without having to get up and check the mail, even though the mail already came. It's not because I'm in some fantastic mood, it's just because my body won't let me sit there. So yeah, no periods of feeling unusually happy or anything like that. Just this constant, relentless need to be moving, moving, moving.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often have trouble keeping your focus on tasks or conversations, or find yourself easily distracted?
turns.patient_response:
Focus? Yeah, that's... well, it's a whole thing. I try, I really do try to pay attention, especially when it's important stuff. Like, take the other day, for example. My sister came over, and she was trying to coordinate who was taking granddad to his appointments, right? The ride times, what we needed to pick up for the pantry—because he's very particular about his brand of oatmeal and those little fruit cups he likes—and then something about the church bake sale or whatever plans she had for Sunday. 

And I'm sitting there, and I start off listening good. I'm nodding, I'm locking in on the ride times—Tuesday at 2:00, Thursday at 9:30, got it. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just decides it's heard enough and goes on a little vacation. She's still talking, her mouth is moving, but my mind just slips right off. I start looking at the smudge on the coffee table, thinking I need to grab the Windex, and then I'm wondering if I left the garage door open, and before I know it, she's looking at me waiting for an answer about who's picking up the oatmeal. 

And I have to be like, "Wait, what did you say about Thursday?" And she gets so mad, doc. She thinks I don't care, but I do! I just... I miss pieces. Big pieces that I really needed to hear. It's like trying to hold water in your hands, you know? You start off with a full handful, but it just leaks out through your fingers no matter how tight you squeeze. So yeah, keeping focus on conversations, especially when there's a lot of details being thrown at me... it's a real struggle. I just can't seem to stay tuned in for the whole broadcast.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states that keeping focus on conversations is a real struggle and they cannot stay tuned in for the whole duration.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes their mind slipping off while someone is speaking directly to them, causing them to miss important pieces of the conversation.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli and unrelated thoughts, such as noticing a smudge on the table or wondering about the garage door.

turns.doctor_question: Before you were twelve years old, did you have similar difficulties sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man. Before I was twelve? Yeah. Honestly, it’s always been exactly like this. I remember back when I was a little boy in school—like, way back, second grade, third grade, all the way up until I eventually stopped going entirely—it was the exact same story every single year. 

My teachers, they were always moving my seat. Like, constantly playing musical chairs with me. First they’d put me in the back so I wouldn't distract the others, but I couldn't stay put back there. I'd be tipping my chair back or wandering over to look at the class pet or whatever. So then they’d move me right up to the very front row, right under the chalkboard, thinking they could keep a closer eye on me. But then I’d just be turning around backwards in my seat, talking out of turn to the kids behind me, just blurting stuff out right in the middle of a math lesson or spelling or whatever we were supposed to be focusing on. 

I just could not stay put for the life of me. I’d be sitting there, and my legs would get that exact same restless feeling I was telling you about earlier, and I’d just jump up. The bell wouldn't have even rung yet, class wasn't even close to being done, and I'd just be out of my seat heading for the pencil sharpener or going to look out the window because I heard a truck drive by. I got in so much trouble for jumping up before class was done. They’d make me stand in the hall, or they'd send these long, angry notes home to my folks... 

It was exhausting for the teachers, I'm sure, but it was just how I was built. They tried putting my desk by the door, by the window, right next to the teacher's desk, but none of it ever worked because the problem wasn't where I was sitting, you know? The problem was that they expected me to sit at all for hours on end. I just couldn't do it. So yeah, even back when I was a little kid, seven or eight years old, it was exactly like this. Just constantly in motion, constantly getting yelled at to sit down and be quiet.
